MicroburstHunter · data-centre networks

Fifty milliseconds of chaos, caught in twenty.

Somewhere in a calm aisle of servers, one host suddenly shouts — 150 Mbps for 50 ms — and every other flow in the switch pays for it. This system hears the shout while it is still happening, names the host behind it, and turns its volume down in the kernel.

Where it starts

One port. One host.
Fifty milliseconds of noise.

A microburst isn’t a flood that builds — it’s a spike that lands all at once. Host 10.0.0.99 pushes 150 Mbps into switch S1, the buffer starts filling instantly, and flows that did nothing wrong begin to queue behind it.

Burst150 Mbps · 50 ms

Why it matters

Too fast to see.
Too sharp to ignore.

Most monitoring polls every second, or every few seconds. A 50 ms burst lives and dies between two polls — the dashboard shows a calm green line while, inside the switch, the buffer filled, packets queued, and latency spiked for everyone sharing that fabric.

MicroburstHunter works at the timescale of the problem itself. It watches traffic window by window, keeps a running EWMA average, and reacts inside the event — detection at 20 ms, attribution to the host causing it, and a kernel-level cap that lands on that host alone. Then, when the aisle is quiet again, it stands down and keeps watching.

The stakes

What fifty milliseconds
can break

A burst is short. Its blast radius isn’t. Everything sharing switch S1 pays for one host’s 50 ms — and if nobody catches it, it just happens again.

Packets drop

The switch buffer is finite. While 10.0.0.99 fires at 150 Mbps, the buffer fills — and once it is full, arriving packets have nowhere to go. They are dropped, and the flows they belonged to stall and retransmit into the same congestion.

Calls break up

Voice and video are just flows sharing the fabric. Queued behind the spike, their packets arrive late and out of order — on the call, that is robotic audio, frozen frames, and two people talking over the wreckage of each other’s sentences.

Transactions stall

A request that should clear in milliseconds waits behind the burst instead. Timeouts fire, retries pile onto an already-full buffer, and one host’s 50 ms turns into somebody else’s failed transaction.

And if nobody catches it

Second-by-second monitoring polls straight past a 50 ms event — the dashboard stays green while it repeats, unseen. Caught at 20 ms and capped at ~35 Mbps, the same burst becomes a non-event: in the live kernel test, 92.2 Mbps offered arrived as 33.9 Mbps received.

The moment it gets caught

20 ms

From the first window over the line to the flag going up. The burst runs for 50 ms — at 20, the Hunter is already moving: naming the host, reaching for the kernel, turning one sender down while every other flow sails on.

Under the hood

Five stages, one very
short gauntlet

Every burst runs the same path through the system. The stages light up in turn — this is the real architecture, not a diagram of one.

Detect — an average that notices

An exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA, α = 0.1) tracks the traffic rate window by window against an 80 Mbps threshold. When the burst lands, the average crosses the line at the second window — the flag goes up 20 ms in, while the burst is still on the wire.

The signal that matters
Flag up in 20 ms
Capture → Detect → Attribute → Mitigate → PresentPython / Scapy · Linux tc · React + Convex

Inside the backend

From wire to verdict,
in twenty milliseconds

This is the real pipeline, playing itself. Packets stream in off the wire, Scapy slices them into windows, an EWMA average watches for the spike — and when host 10.0.0.99 fires at 150 Mbps, the whole chain reacts before the burst is even over.

From the bench

Measured, not marketed

The detector

EWMA with α = 0.1 against an 80 Mbps threshold. In benchmarking it caught 100 / 100 microbursts with 0 false positives in 1,000 windows.

The cap

Linux tc/HTB shapes the offender to ~35 Mbps. On the live kernel test, 92.2 Mbps offered became 33.9 Mbps received — within a few percent of the cap doing exactly its job.

The stack

Capture in Python + Scapy, mitigation in the Linux kernel, console in React + Convex. Built as a Computer Networks course project — the full system is on GitHub.
